content:
Caring for someone with arthritis and frailty can be tiring. Breaks help carers stay well.

This guide explains options. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Types of respite

  • Day centres.
  • Sitting services at home.
  • Home care.
  • Short stays in a care home.

Carer's assessment

Any carer can ask the local council for a carer's assessment. It looks at your needs and support.

Paying for respite

The council may contribute after assessment. Some charities also help.

Planning a break

Book early, share medicines and routines, and plan the return.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Do I have to be a full-time carer?

No, any carer can ask for an assessment.

Is respite only in care homes?

No.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: Help and support for carers
  • Community Transport Association

Educational information for people in the United Kingdom — not a diagnosis or personal medical advice. Charity no. 1218461. Reviewed by Louis Maxwell (HCPC PH128483). Living With Arthritis is an independent charity and is not part of Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis). Everyone's situation is different, so follow the advice of your own GP and care team. If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111 (NHS 24 on 111 in Scotland; in Northern Ireland, your GP or GP out-of-hours service).
